paper.title: Personality change following psychological trauma: disentangling traits, personality functioning, and personality disorder.
paper.summary:
PURPOSE OF REVIEW: Trauma survivors often describe themselves as changed, but this experience can reflect several different processes. This review considers change in broad personality traits, changes in how traits are expressed, developmental influences on emerging personality, and changes in personality functioning.
RECENT FINDINGS: Longitudinal studies show that personality remains relatively stable while changing across development. Broad trait changes after major negative life events are usually small at the group level, although individual responses vary. During adolescence, temperament and character show continuity alongside ongoing change. Recent work suggests that personality functioning may be more labile than broad traits. Process models from personality science offer a plausible, but not yet trauma-specific, account of how repeated states can become more enduring through reinforcement, generalization, and integration into self-understanding.
SUMMARY: The clinically useful question is not simply whether trauma changes personality, but what has changed, when the change occurred, and how broadly it extends across contexts. Trauma may alter trait expression, contribute to smaller trait shifts, disturb identity and relationships, or, when exposure is prolonged and developmentally embedded, influence the course through which personality becomes organized. Personality disorder should be reserved for pervasive and enduring dysfunction rather than inferred from trauma exposure alone.

paper.title: Physical distancing to prevent influenza-like illness on a college campus: The eX-FLU trial.
paper.summary: Public health recommendations often advise people to isolate when infected with influenza-like illness (ILI) with the goal of promoting physical distancing and limiting face-to-face interactions when risk of transmission is highest. Because isolation may have negative consequences, it is important to carefully assess whether encouragement to physically distance actually prevents cases of ILI. College campuses can be especially vulnerable to outbreaks of ILI and are ideal environments for assessing the impact of encouragement-to-physically-distance interventions. The eX-FLU cluster-randomized trial followed 579 students on a college campus over a ten-week period during flu season to evaluate such an intervention. Students in the trial were randomized to receive the intervention-encouragement to isolate in their dorm room when symptomatic for ILI-or control. Evaluating the effect of this intervention is challenging because of dependence between students in the trial and an anticipated spillover effect of the intervention. Moreover, while the intervention was designed to affect both face-to-face interactions and ILI infections, the effect on ILI infections is of primary public health interest. In this paper, a randomization-based testing procedure is proposed to assess the intervention effect specifically on ILI infections in the presence of dependent data and spillover effects. The testing procedure is shown theoretically and empirically to control the type I error rate and have good statistical power to detect an intervention effect in trials similar to eX-FLU. When applied to the eX-FLU data, this testing procedure gives moderate evidence that the intervention reduced ILI infections.

paper.title: PPP1R1B differentially modulates alcohol intake and emotional comorbidity through distinct prefrontal circuits.
paper.summary: Excessive alcohol consumption frequently co-occurs with anxiety and depression in alcohol use disorder (AUD), yet the specific neural circuits and molecular mechanisms coordinating these comorbid conditions remain poorly defined. The medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC), particularly its prelimbic (PL) and infralimbic (IL) subregions, projects to key reward and emotion centers like the nucleus accumbens (Nac) and basolateral amygdala (BLA), but the functional heterogeneity of these projections is unclear. Using chemogenetics, retrograde tracing, electrophysiology, spatial proteomics, and cell-type-specific gene editing in mice subjected to a 4-wk intermittent access to alcohol (IAA) paradigm, we selectively manipulated glutamatergic projections from the PL and IL to the Nac core, Nac shell, and BLA and assessed alcohol intake, anxiety-like, and depression-like behaviors. Chemogenetic activation of PL-Nac core projections reduced short-term alcohol intake, anxiety-, and depression-like behaviors, while IL-BLA activation decreased alcohol consumption and anxiety-like behaviors only. Retrograde tracing revealed mirror-image anatomical segregation of projection-defined neuronal subpopulations within PL/IL linking spatial organization to functional divergence. IAA induced pathway-specific synaptic adaptations. Spatial proteomics nominated protein phosphatase 1 regulatory subunit 1B (PPP1R1B) as a candidate molecule in PL-Nac core neurons. Independent immunostaining confirmed PPP1R1B downregulation, and circuit-specific knockout recapitulated alcohol-related and affective phenotypes, whereas overexpression reversed them. In IL-BLA neurons, PPP1R1B manipulation modulated alcohol intake and anxiety, but not depression. These findings define a subregion- and projection-specific organizational logic in the mPFC for differentially regulating alcohol consumption and emotional comorbidity, with PPP1R1B as a key molecular determinant. This provides a neural pathway-molecule framework for targeted intervention in AUD.

paper.title: Patient willingness to de-escalate adjuvant therapy based on predictive biomarker results in stage IIB-IIID melanoma: A cross-sectional survey.
paper.summary:
INTRODUCTION: Predictive biomarkers such as circulating tumour DNA (ctDNA) and gene expression profiling (GEP) may guide adjuvant melanoma therapy de-escalation by identifying low-recurrence-risk patients. However, their implementation depends on patient willingness to act on test results. This study investigated patient preferences regarding predictive biomarkers.
METHODS: A cross-sectional survey was conducted among consecutive patients with AJCC 8th-edition stages IIB-IIID melanoma at a tertiary centre (N = 159, response rate 80.7%). The self-constructed questionnaire assessed biomarker-related attitudes, including willingness to forgo adjuvant therapy, accuracy thresholds, and undertreatment-overtreatment trade-offs, alongside sociodemographic characteristics. Validated instruments assessed decision-making preferences (Control Preferences Scale), health literacy (HLS-EU-Q16), fear of progression (PA-F-KF), and anxiety (GAD-7). Alongside descriptive analyses, logistic regression examined factors associated with willingness to forgo therapy.
RESULTS: Despite limited prior awareness (34.2%), 97.4% considered biomarker research important. Most patients expected personalised therapy (82.3%) as primary benefit and wished to receive prognostic information on adverse events (91.1%) and disease progression (83.5%). Given a favourable five-year test result, 38.0% would forgo adjuvant therapy; 73.3% required ≥ 95% test accuracy. Two-thirds (66.9%) considered undertreatment worse than overtreatment; only 18.3% would accept de-escalation given a 10% false-negative rate. Lower health literacy (OR 0.61, p = 0.045) and an academic degree (OR 2.31, p = 0.037) were associated with willingness to forgo therapy. The latter emerged only after adjustment for health literacy, potentially reflecting a suppression effect.
CONCLUSIONS: Melanoma patients demonstrate strong interest in biomarkers but demand high accuracy with low tolerance for false-negative predictions. Implementation of biomarker-guided decisions requires targeted patient education addressing predictive uncertainty.

paper.title: Valence-dependent functional connectivity during vicarious observation of hostile and affiliative social interactions.
paper.summary: Social environment profoundly influences well-being, yet the neural correlates of vicariously observing workplace interactions across the emotional spectrum remain underexplored. This study investigated valence-dependent patterns of functional connectivity (FC) during observation of hostile and affiliative customer-employee encounters in thirty-four healthy adults. Seed-based FC analysis examined the connectivity of key regions associated with empathy and relational social cognitive processing, and region-of-interest (ROI)-to-ROI analysis evaluated the configuration of three core brain networks. Results revealed that witnessing hostility, compared to affiliation, was associated with greater connectivity within the salience network, a system typically involved in vigilance, and increased coupling between core empathy regions and sensory areas. Conversely, relative to hostile conditions, observing affiliation was associated with greater integration within the default mode and frontoparietal networks. Furthermore, exploratory analysis revealed that emotion regulation strategies were associated with these pathways, in which cognitive reappraisal was linked to reduced empathy-sensory coupling during hostility, while expressive suppression was associated with broadly reduced empathy-related connectivity particularly during positive observation. These findings indicate that functional brain organization differs depending on the valence of observed social interactions, with potential relevance for understanding how workplace social dynamics may influence neural processing. This work bridges social neuroscience with organizational behavior, highlighting directions for future research on vicarious stress and well-being.

paper.title: Photobiomodulation therapy and the regulation of excitation-inhibition balance in neurological and psychiatric disorders: Mechanistic and translational perspectives.
paper.summary: Photobiomodulation therapy (PBMT) has emerged as a promising non-invasive intervention capable of modulating biological processes through the application of non-ionizing light in the red to near-infrared spectrum. Increasing evidence suggests that PBMT may influence central nervous system (CNS) function through effects on mitochondrial activity, neurovascular coupling, and neuroimmune pathways. There is evidence that PBMT can attenuate cellular and molecular alterations and improve functional outcomes in different pathologies of the nervous system. Given that excitation-inhibition imbalance is a core pathophysiological mechanism underlying several neurological and psychiatric disorders, understanding the mechanistic and clinical effects of PBMT on neural network regulation is of growing scientific interest. This narrative review aims to synthesize mechanistic and translational evidence regarding the effects of PBMT on mechanisms relevant to excitation-inhibition regulation across neurological and psychiatric conditions. To our knowledge, this is the first review to specifically examine PBMT through the framework of excitation-inhibition balance across neurological and psychiatric disorders. Experimental studies have reported reductions in oxidative stress and neuroinflammation, attenuation of glutamatergic excitotoxicity and neuronal apoptosis, preservation of interneuron integrity, modulation of astrocytic function, and stimulation of neurogenesis. Early clinical findings suggest improvements in cognitive performance, mood symptoms, motor function, and behavioral outcomes. Overall, PBMT may influence mechanisms relevant to excitation-inhibition regulation through integrated mitochondrial, vascular, and immune mechanisms, supporting its potential as a systems-level neuromodulatory approach. Further research is required to consolidate translational evidence and clarify its potential role in clinical practice.

paper.title: Biological mechanisms underlying avoidant/restrictive food intake disorder (ARFID).
paper.summary: Avoidant/restrictive food intake disorder (ARFID) is a complex eating disorder characterized by persistent avoidance or restriction of food intake that is not driven by concerns about body weight or shape. ARFID is characterized by an extremely low food intake and may be driven by sensory aversions to certain foods, a low interest in food, and/or traumatic experiences related to food intake, leading to avoidance. Although ARFID has a number of specific criteria and symptoms, many aspects of its diagnosis, development, and treatment remain unclear. In this narrative review, we summarize the available evidence on molecular, cellular, and neurobiological mechanisms potentially underlying the core manifestations of ARFID, including food avoidance and restriction, sensory-based food aversion, and fear of aversive consequences. The potential mechanisms discussed include altered sensory processing, dysregulation of hunger and satiety signals, conditioned taste aversion and other forms of associative learning, alterations in the microbiome-gut-brain axis, immune mechanisms, and genetic factors. Because direct evidence from ARFID populations remains limited, we also consider findings from related but diagnostically distinct conditions and phenotypes, including picky or selective eating, food neophobia, and sensory food aversion. Such findings may provide insights into mechanisms relevant to ARFID but cannot be assumed to be specific to the disorder. By integrating evidence across these biological domains, this review aims to identify potential mechanisms underlying the heterogeneous manifestations of ARFID and highlight priorities for future research.

paper.title: Ketamine enhances ketogenic diet-induced resilience to activity-based anorexia of adult mice through hippocampal synaptic plasticity.
paper.summary: Ketogenic diet (KGD) combined with ketamine (KET) suppresses food restriction-evoked hyperactivity in activity-based anorexia (ABA) mouse model of anorexia nervosa (AN) for more than 28 days, thereby improving weight retention and reducing anxiety, even after mice return to standard diet (SD) and are re-challenged with ABA (KGD + KET → SD, "KET + KGD group"). Suppression of these AN-like behavior is not sustained in mice fed KGD without KET (KGD → SD, "KGD-only group"). We hypothesized that the sustained efficacy of KET + KGD is associated with altered prevalence of certain synapses in the dorsal hippocampus that influence behavior. We compared the prevalence of excitatory and inhibitory synapses between KET + KGD (N = 7) versus KGD-only (N = 7) groups, using electron microscopy and GAD immunolabeling to distinguish GABAergic inhibitory synapses from non-GABAergic excitatory synapses. Pyramidal cell layer (PCL) was analyzed to assess the contribution by parvalbumin + subtype of GABAergic neurons known to reside there, while stratum lacunosum-molecular (SLM) was analyzed to assess inhibition by non-PV + GABAergic neurons known to reside there. In both PCL and SLM, the KET + KGD group exhibited greater correlation between GABAergic inhibition of PNs and weight retention. In SLM of the KET + KGD group, the areal density of excitatory synapses was less. Inhibitory synapses onto GABAergic dendrites (disinhibition which may also augment excitability) correlated negatively with hyperactivity for the KET + KGD group only. KET + KGD, but not KGD-only, may sustain ABA resilience by enhancing plasticity of both glutamatergic and GABAergic synapses. This jointly sustained plasticity underlying hippocampal excitability may be the cellular bases for KET + KGD treatment's suppression of AN relapses.

paper.title: Domain adaptation spatial feature perception neural network for cross-subject EEG emotion recognition
paper.summary: Emotion recognition is a critical research topic within affective computing, with potential applications across various domains. Currently, EEG-based emotion recognition, utilizing deep learning frameworks, has been effectively applied and achieved commendable performance. However, existing deep learning-based models face challenges in capturing both the spatial activity features and spatial topology features of EEG signals simultaneously. To address this challenge, a domain-adaptation spatial-feature perception-network has been proposed for cross-subject EEG emotion recognition tasks, named DSP-EmotionNet. Firstly, a spatial activity topological feature extractor module has been designed to capture spatial activity features and spatial topology features of EEG signals, named SATFEM. Then, using SATFEM as the feature extractor, DSP-EmotionNet has been designed, significantly improving the accuracy of the model in cross-subject EEG emotion recognition tasks. The proposed model surpasses state-of-the-art methods in cross-subject EEG emotion recognition tasks, achieving an average recognition accuracy of 82.5% on the SEED dataset and 65.9% on the SEED-IV dataset.
